_**Agent (claude-sonnet-5 2026-09-28 17:44:40Z)**_

`specstory run claude` is explicitly a **terminal/interactive-mode wrapper** ("Launch terminal coding agents in interactive mode") — it spawns the `claude` CLI binary as a subprocess and captures its terminal I/O. It has no concept of the VSCode chat pane you're using now; that's a separate extension UI/IPC layer that specstory doesn't hook into. So it would only give you the command-line REPL experience, not this pane.

One more wrinkle: I ran `specstory check` and it currently can't find the Claude Code binary at all:

```
❌ Claude Code check failed!
  Error: 🔍 Could not find Claude Code at: claude
```

So even in a terminal, `specstory run claude` would fail right now unless you point it at the right binary with `-c "/path/to/claude"`, or it gets installed/linked as `claude` on PATH.

Given that:
- If you want logging, it'll mean working in a plain terminal REPL, not this chat pane
- It currently needs a path fix (`-c`) or install to work at all

<tool-use data-tool-type="write" data-tool-name="Write"><details>
<summary>Tool use: **Write**</summary>

```markdown
## Summary

When users click into a drill-down report (e.g. Net Worth, Cash Flow, Spending) from the reports overview, they are navigated to `/reports/:id` via the app's router. Returning to the overview currently requires a mouse click on a back button — there's no keyboard equivalent, even though other parts of the app (autocomplete dropdowns, the search box, date pickers) already treat Escape as a "dismiss/back out" key. Adding a scoped Escape handler to report drill-down pages would make that navigation pattern consistent across the app.

## User Story

As a user exploring my financial reports, I want to press the Escape key to back out of a drill-down report page so that I can navigate through my data quickly using my keyboard.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. While viewing a report drill-down page (any route under `/reports/:id` reached from the reports overview), pressing Escape navigates back to the reports overview.
2. Escape does **not** trigger this navigation when a modal, dropdown, popover, autocomplete, or date picker is open and already consuming Escape for its own dismissal (several components — `Autocomplete.tsx`, `Search.tsx`, `DateSelect.tsx` — already handle Escape locally; the new listener must not fire on top of or instead of those).
3. Escape has no effect on the reports overview page itself (nothing to back out of there).
4. The feature works via keyboard alone — no mouse interaction needed to trigger or verify it.

## Out of Scope

- Escape handling on non-report pages (budget, accounts, etc.).
- Any change to Escape behavior already implemented in modals, autocompletes, or dropdowns elsewhere in the app.
- A generalized/global keyboard shortcut system — this is one scoped listener for report drill-down pages.

## Open Questions

1. Should Escape use browser history back (`navigate(-1)`), or navigate explicitly to the reports overview route? History back could send a user somewhere unexpected if they arrived at the report from outside the reports section (e.g. a deep link); an explicit route may be more predictable.
2. Reports render through `ReportsDashboardRouter`/`Overview.tsx` using `useNavigate` — is there one shared parent component drill-down pages pass through where a single listener can live, or does each report page need it added individually?
3. Should Escape be suppressed while focus is inside a text input on the report page (e.g. a filter field), or should it still back out? Worth deciding explicitly rather than leaving it to whatever the browser does by default.

## Rough Scope

Small — Report navigation already goes through React Router (`useNavigate`, routes at `/reports/:id`), so this is fundamentally one keydown listener plus routing logic that already exists elsewhere in the app. The only real risk is conflicting with the several components that already claim Escape for their own dismissal behavior (open question #2 above is the key thing to nail down before writing code).

## Source

Messing around with the application, I got slightly annoyed by not being able to quickly go back to the report page, so I thought this might be a nice feature.
```

<tool-use data-tool-type="write" data-tool-name="Write"><details>
<summary>Tool use: **Write**</summary>

```markdown
## Summary

Users tracking long-term financial targets (a vacation fund, an emergency fund, a specific savings goal) currently have no dynamic way to see progress toward that target on the dashboard — only static text in a Notes widget. Actual's dashboard already supports a generic, extensible widget model (`AbstractWidget<type, meta>` in `packages/loot-core/src/types/models/dashboard.ts`), and existing widgets like Net Worth, Cash Flow, and Spending already compute live values from a set of transaction-filter conditions (`RuleConditionEntity[]`) plus a time frame. A "Personal Goal" widget would follow that same pattern: a target amount plus a set of filter conditions, rendered as a progress bar showing how far the filtered transaction total is toward the target.

Note: the widget persistence layer (`packages/loot-core/src/server/dashboard/app.ts`) is already generic across widget types — adding a new widget type does **not** require new backend endpoints, just a new `type` + `meta` shape that flows through the existing CRUD.

## User Story

As a user planning my financial targets, I want to add a dashboard widget that shows progress toward a savings goal — based on a target amount and a set of transaction filters — so that I can monitor my goal completion over time without manually updating static notes.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A new widget type (e.g. `goal-card`) can be added to the dashboard from the existing "add widget" menu in `Overview.tsx`, alongside Net Worth, Cash Flow, Spending, etc.
2. The widget's settings include, at minimum: a target amount, a set of transaction-filter conditions (reusing `RuleConditionEntity[]` the way `NetWorthWidget`/`CashFlowWidget`/`SpendingWidget` already do), and a time frame.
3. The widget displays a progress bar showing (sum of matching transactions) / (target amount), plus the raw current total and target amount as text.
4. Progress values are computed using the app's existing summary/filter calculation logic (the same spreadsheet-style computation `SummaryCard.tsx` / `GetCardData.tsx` use for other widgets) — no new calculation engine.
5. The widget visually distinguishes at least two states: goal in progress vs. goal complete (100%+). Anything beyond that (e.g. "near completion") is left to the implementer's judgment unless Open Question #2 below is resolved first.
6. Widget settings persist across sessions using the existing generic dashboard widget storage (no new backend work required per the note above).
7. The widget matches Actual's existing dashboard card visual conventions (sizing, fonts, currency formatting) as used by the other report cards.

## Out of Scope

- A history/trend view of goal progress over time (this is a point-in-time progress card, not a report).
- Multiple simultaneous goals sharing one widget — each widget instance tracks one goal (add more widgets for more goals, same as other widget types).
- New backend endpoints or a new persistence mechanism — this must ride on the existing generic widget CRUD.
- Notifications or alerts when a goal is reached.

## Open Questions

1. Where does the user configure the target amount and filter conditions — inline on the dashboard card itself, or by drilling into a dedicated full-page view the way Net Worth/Cash Flow/Spending each have both a full report page (e.g. `NetWorth.tsx`) and a condensed dashboard card (e.g. `CashFlowCard.tsx`)? This significantly affects scope: a full page + card pair is considerably more work than an inline-editable card alone.
2. What color/visual states are wanted beyond "in progress" vs. "complete" — e.g. a distinct state for over-target, or a red state if a deadline is added and missed? (Note: this issue doesn't currently define a deadline/target-date concept at all — only a target amount. If time-bound goals are wanted, that's an additional meta field and UI affordance to decide on now rather than after implementation starts.)
3. Should this be scoped down to just the read-only progress card (seeded with a manually-constructed widget for now), with the settings-editing UI split into a separate follow-up issue? Given the number of touchpoints (widget type definition, dispatch wiring, add-widget menu entry, progress card UI, and a settings editor), splitting could make each piece independently deliverable and testable rather than one large PR.

## Rough Scope

Large — Despite the dashboard widget architecture already being generic (no new backend endpoints, no new persistence mechanism), this still touches: a new widget type + meta definition, registration in the add-widget menu and the `Overview.tsx` render dispatch, a new card component with a progress bar and conditional styling, reuse of the existing filter/summary calculation logic, and (pending Open Question #1) potentially a full settings-editing UI. For a beginner team, following the Net Worth/Cash Flow/Spending widgets as a concrete template will help, but the number of files touched keeps this Large rather than Medium. Consider splitting per Open Question #3.

## Source

Community feature request / GitHub issue discussion.
```
